title: Hello, what's your name?
title_target: Kumusta ka? Ano ang pangalan mo?
goal: Greet people at the right time of day, give your name and where you're from, ask how someone is, and use *po* from the very first sentence.
bekal: greet with *magandang umaga/hapon/gabi* at the right moments
give your name with *ako si* and ask someone else's
add *po* to be polite without changing anything else

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Unang araw sa Maynila
dialogs.intro: First day in Manila. Budi has just stepped off the plane and meets Ana, a language-school staff member who has come to pick him up.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Magandang umaga po! Ako si Ana.
lines.literal: beautiful-of morning sir! I si Ana.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Magandang umaga rin po. Ako si Budi.
lines.id: Good morning to you too, ma'am. I'm Budi.
lines.literal: beautiful-of morning also ma'am. I si Budi.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Fine, thank you, ma'am. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: I'm fine too. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia, ma'am. From Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Ang layo! Nag-aaral ka ba ng Tagalog?
lines.id: So far away! Are you studying Tagalog?

lines.text: Opo, nag-aaral po ako. Konti pa lang.
lines.id: Yes, ma'am, I'm studying. Just a little so far.
lines.literal: yes-ma'am, studying ma'am I. little still only.

lines.text: Ang galing mo! Masaya akong makilala ka.
lines.id: Well done! Nice to meet you.

notes: **Kumusta comes from Spanish.** It was originally *¿Cómo está?* — "how are you". That's why it doesn't look like other Tagalog words, and why it never changes form: *kumusta ka*, *kumusta po kayo*, *kumusta si Ana*. One form for everyone.

**The standard answer is *mabuti*.** It means "good" and almost always travels with *naman*: *mabuti naman*. Without *naman* the answer sounds flat, like filling in a form; with it, it sounds like real conversation. Particles like this get full treatment in unit 14.

**Po is the whole Tagalog politeness system in one syllable.** It has no meaning of its own and changes no grammar — you just slip it into the sentence. Use *po* with older people, people you've just met, officials, anyone you respect. Leaving it out isn't a grammar mistake, it's a bad impression.

**Opo isn't just "yes".** *Oo* is plain "yes"; *opo* is polite "yes". They aren't interchangeable: answering *oo* to an elder in the Philippines sounds like saying "yeah" in a bored tone to your boss's mother.

**Ako si Budi has no verb.** Literally it's just "I si Budi". Like many languages (Russian, Arabic), Tagalog doesn't need a word like "am/is" to link two things. What Tagalog does add is the marker *si* in front of a person's name — and it's mandatory.

**Taga- attaches to a place name** and means "person from". *Taga-Jakarta*, *taga-Maynila*, *taga-Cebu*. The hyphen is used when the next word is a proper name; with ordinary nouns it's written together: *tagabundok* (mountain person).

**Ang layo, ang galing** — the word *ang* here is not the marker you'll learn in unit 2, but an exclamation: "how …!" Compare *ang ganda!* (so pretty!), *ang init!* (so hot!). This pattern is very common and very easy: *ang* + adjective, done.

**Walang anuman** literally means "there is nothing" — the standard reply to "thank you". In casual talk people often answer more briefly: *sige* (okay) or even *no problem* in English. All three are normal.
**Tara na** is the most characteristically Filipino invitation: "let's go". It almost always appears with *na*. If you memorize only one invitation from this course, make it this one.

grammars.title: Introductions — no verb needed
body: Introductions use the simplest pattern in the whole language: two things placed side by side, with no linking word.
after: Notice the order: **the description first, the person after**. *Guro ako*, not *ako guro*. This is the opposite of English and will keep recurring throughout the course — Tagalog almost always puts the "news" first.

*Ako ay si Budi* is also correct and you may have seen it in old books. *Ay* flips the order to look like English, but it sounds formal, like a speech or a newspaper. People don't use it in conversation.
⚠️ *Si* is only for **people's names**. For things, use *ang*: *Ang bahay*, not *si bahay*. These markers are set up in units 2 and 5.

grammars.title: Po and opo — one syllable that changes everything
body: Tagalog has no layered speech levels like Javanese or Korean. All it has are two small words, and both work by attaching.
after: Two things change when you're polite: **po** is slipped in, and **ka/mo** rise to **kayo/ninyo** — the plural forms used as a respectful singular, exactly like *vous* in French.

*Po* almost always goes **after the first word** of the sentence. *Salamat po*, *Hindi po ako guro*, *Taga-saan po kayo?* When in doubt, put it after the first word and you'll be right nine times out of ten.
There's also *ho* — a more relaxed version of *po*, used with people only slightly older or about your age. As a newcomer, stick with *po*: being too polite is never a problem in the Philippines.

blocks.text: These twelve sentences aren't grammar to memorize — they're emergency tools. Learn the whole phrase now; understand its structure later.

blocks.text: *Pasensya na* literally means "patience now" — from Spanish *paciencia*. For a deeper apology there is *paumanhin po*, but it sounds formal; in daily life *pasensya na po* covers nearly everything.

blocks.title: One sentence that will change your experience in the Philippines
items: *Nag-aaral po ako ng Tagalog. Puwede po bang mag-Tagalog tayo?* — "I'm studying Tagalog. May we speak Tagalog?"

The typical difficulty of learning Tagalog isn't that people are harsh, but the opposite: almost every Filipino speaks English and will switch to it automatically as soon as they hear your accent, thinking they're helping. The sentence above politely stops them — and is almost always met with a smile, because foreigners who want to learn Tagalog are still rare.

blocks.text: Notice that all the time-of-day greetings follow the same pattern: *maganda* (beautiful) + the linker **-ng** + the name of the time. That linker is called a *linker*, and it appears in nearly every unit of this course. Its rules are set up in unit 3.

To answer a greeting, just repeat it and add *rin* or *din* ("too"): *Magandang umaga rin po*. It's written *rin* after a word ending in a vowel and *din* after a consonant — a leftover of the d→r sound rule you saw on the pronunciation page.

blocks.title: Words for addressing people
items: **Ate** (AH-teh, older sister) and **Kuya** (KOO-yah, older brother) are used for anyone slightly older — restaurant staff, drivers, shopkeepers. They aren't only family terms but everyday polite forms of address.
**Tita / Tito** for people the age of your parents, **Lola / Lolo** for the age of your grandparents.
**Ma'am / Sir** are widely used in English, especially in shops and offices. There's nothing odd about mixing: *Salamat po, ma'am.*
